entry.sum: Adding puts amounts together and subtracting takes an amount away, finds a missing part or compares two amounts: $3 + 2 = 5$ and $5 - 2 = 3$. Subtraction undoes addition, so every subtraction is a missing-number addition. Small sums are found by counting on, making a ten and doubles; bigger ones by adding tens to tens and ones to ones, making or breaking a ten when needed.

blocks.body:
Three birds sit on a fence and two more fly down to join them. How many birds are there now? Then two birds fly away. How many are left? Questions like these are about adding and subtracting.

Adding puts amounts together. Subtracting takes an amount away, or finds how much is left, or how many more one amount has than another. On this page you will learn what the signs $+$, $-$ and $=$ mean, how to add and subtract by counting on and counting back, why subtraction undoes addition, how to use a ten to add and subtract within 20, how to solve story problems, and how tens and hundreds let you add and subtract bigger numbers.

You need to know how to split a number into parts ([[composing-decomposing-numbers]]) and what tens and ones are ([[place-value]]).

blocks.title: What adding and subtracting mean
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to act out an adding or subtracting story with objects, and write it with the signs $+$, $-$ and $=$.

Try this. Put 3 cups on the table. Put 2 more cups next to them. Count all the cups. Now take 2 cups away. Count the cups that are left.

When you put the cups together you were adding. When you took cups away you were subtracting. Children first add and subtract like this, with real things, with fingers, or with drawings, and only later with written signs.

blocks.title: Plus, minus and equals
blocks.body:
The sign $+$ is read "plus". $3 + 2$ means 3 and 2 put together. The numbers we add are called addends, and the answer is the sum or total: the sum of 3 and 2 is 5.

The sign $-$ is read "minus" (or "take away"). $5 - 2$ means 2 taken away from 5. The answer is called the difference: the difference of 5 and 2 is 3.

The sign $=$ is read "equals" or "is the same as". $3 + 2 = 5$ says that 3 + 2 is the same number as 5. A number sentence with an equals sign, such as $3 + 2 = 5$, is called an equation.

blocks.title: Four kinds of adding and subtracting stories
blocks.body:
Most adding and subtracting stories are of four kinds.

1. Add to: something is added. 3 birds sit on a fence and 2 more come. Now there are $3 + 2 = 5$.
2. Take from: something is taken away. 5 birds sit on a fence and 2 fly off. Now there are $5 - 2 = 3$.
3. Put together or take apart: two parts make a whole, and nothing moves. 3 red cups and 2 blue cups make $3 + 2 = 5$ cups.
4. Compare: two amounts are set side by side. Ana has 5 cups and Ben has 3. Ana has $5 - 3 = 2$ more.

So subtracting is not only taking away. It also finds a missing part, and how many more or how many fewer.

blocks.title: One story, many ways: 5 take away 2

items.label: Objects
items.body: Put out 5 counters, move 2 away, and count the 3 that stay.

items.label: Fingers
items.body: Hold up 5 fingers, fold down 2, and look at the 3 still up.

items.label: Drawing
items.body: Draw 5 circles and cross out 2. Count the 3 that are not crossed out.

items.label: Words
items.body: Five take away two is three.

blocks.body: Five birds sit on a fence and two fly away. The same subtraction can be shown in many ways.

rows.text: The England programme of study speaks of the equals sign (the sign $=$).
The sign $=$ is called the equal sign; a number sentence with it is an equation.

The progressions prefer total to sum with young children, because sum sounds like some, and say the names minuend and subtrahend (the first and second numbers of a subtraction) are not needed from Kindergarten to Grade 2. NCETM's Year 3 outcomes for column subtraction do use both names.

blocks.title: Adding and taking away zero
blocks.body: Adding 0 does not change a number, and taking away 0 does not change it either: $$7 + 0 = 7, \quad 7 - 0 = 7.$$ Taking away all of a number leaves 0: $7 - 7 = 0$.

If you have 7 cups and no more cups come, you still have 7 cups. If you have 7 cups and you take none away, 7 are still there. If you take all 7 away, none are left. (This is one of the properties of addition, studied on [[properties-of-operations]].)

blocks.title: For adults: read = as "is the same as"
blocks.body: If children only ever see the answer straight after the equals sign, many come to read $=$ as "makes" or "now write the answer". The Common Core progressions say that $=$ does not always mean "makes" or "results in": it means "is the same number as". Illustrative Mathematics Grade 1 also asks children to understand the equal sign, especially in missing-number problems. More on this is on [[equality-equal-sign]].
Write the story with numbers and signs, and find the answer: There are 4 apples in a bowl. Dad puts in 3 more. How many apples are in the bowl now?
blocks.solution:
1. This is an add to story: apples are added.
2. Start with 4 apples, then 3 more are put in: $4 + 3$.
3. Count: 4 apples, then five, six, seven. So $4 + 3 = 7$.
4. Answer: there are 7 apples in the bowl.

blocks.body: Write the story with numbers and signs: There are 6 children on the slide. 4 of them go home. How many are still on the slide?
blocks.solution:
1. This is a take from story: children leave.
2. Start with 6, take away 4: $6 - 4$.
3. Draw 6 circles and cross out 4. 2 circles are not crossed out. So $6 - 4 = 2$.
4. Answer: 2 children are still on the slide.

items.a: Eight minus three equals five (or: eight take away three is five).

items.q: What is the sum of 2 and 6?
What is the difference of 9 and 4?
Draw 4 circles and 1 more circle. Write the addition and the answer.
items.hint: Count all the circles you drew.

items.q: Draw 7 circles and cross out 3. Write the subtraction and the answer.
items.hint: Count only the circles that are not crossed out.

items.q: Which kind of story is it (add to, take from, put together, compare)? 5 red balloons and 4 yellow balloons. How many balloons?
items.hint: Does anything move, or are there just two parts?
items.solution: Put together: nothing is added or taken away; two parts make a whole. $5 + 4 = 9$ balloons.

items.q: Which kind of story is it? Mia has 8 stickers and Leo has 5. How many more stickers does Mia have?
items.hint: Two amounts are set side by side.
items.solution: Compare. Match 5 of Mia's stickers with Leo's 5; 3 of hers are not matched. $8 - 5 = 3$ more.

items.hint: Take away nothing; take away everything.
Read the equals sign as "is the same as".
items.solution: Yes. 4 + 2 is 6, so "6 is the same as 4 + 2" is true.

blocks.body:
- Adding puts amounts together; the answer is the sum or total.
- Subtracting takes away, finds a missing part, or compares; the answer is the difference.
- $+$ is plus, $-$ is minus, $=$ means is the same as.
- Stories can be add to, take from, put together or take apart, and compare.
- Adding or taking away 0 leaves a number the same.

blocks.title: Counting on and counting back
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to add by counting on from a number and subtract by counting back or by counting on, and show this with hops on a number line.

Try this. Put 8 counters in a cup and tell a friend there are 8 inside. Put 3 more on the table. How many are there in all? Do you need to tip out the cup and count from one?

blocks.title: Counting all and counting on
blocks.body:
To find $8 + 3$ a young child may count all: one, two, three, ... up to eight for the first group, and then nine, ten, eleven for the second.

Counting on is quicker. Say the first number, eight, and then count the second group: nine, ten, eleven. Keep track of the three counts on fingers. The last number said, eleven, is the sum.

Counting back is the same idea for taking away. To find $11 - 3$, start at eleven and count back three: ten, nine, eight. So $11 - 3 = 8$.

blocks.title: Why counting on works
blocks.body: When you count a group from one, the last number you say tells how many there are. So saying "eight" for the first group already counts it, and you only need to count the second group from nine onwards.

Counting all 8 + 3 counters from one would say one, two, ..., eight for the first 8 counters, and nine, ten, eleven for the other 3. The first eight words are the same every time and end at eight. Counting on simply skips them and starts at eight. The words said for the other 3 counters, nine, ten, eleven, are exactly the same as before, so the answer is the same.

    t = np.linspace(0, np.pi, 40)
    xs = a + (b - a) * (1 - np.cos(t)) / 2
    ax.plot(xs, y + 0.55 * np.sin(t), color=col, lw=1.8, ls=ls)

blocks.title: Subtracting by counting on
blocks.body: To subtract, you can also count on from the smaller number to the larger one. The number of counts is the difference. For $13 - 9$: start at nine and count ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen. That is 4 counts, so $13 - 9 = 4$.

$13 - 9$ asks: 9 and how many more make 13? Counting on from 9 to 13 counts exactly the numbers that are in 13 but not in the first 9. The Common Core progressions say that counting on for subtraction is easier than counting down.

blocks.title: Ways to find 8 + 3

items.label: Count all
items.body: Put out 8 counters and 3 counters, then count every counter from one to eleven.

items.label: Count on
items.body: Say eight, then count three more on fingers: nine, ten, eleven.

items.label: Number line
items.body: Start at 8 on a number line and make 3 hops of one: 9, 10, 11.

items.label: Ten frame
items.body: 8 counters fill most of a ten frame; 2 more fill it to make 10 and 1 is left over, so 11.

blocks.body: Different sources start from different pictures of the same sum.

blocks.title: For adults: start from the larger number
blocks.body: To count on for $2 + 7$ it is easier to start at seven and count two more than to start at two and count seven more. Children can do this once they see that the order of adding does not change the total, which the England programme of study expects in Year 2 (see [[properties-of-operations]]).
Find $6 + 3$ by counting on.
blocks.solution:
1. Say the first number: six.
2. Count three more, raising a finger each time: seven (1), eight (2), nine (3).
3. Three fingers are up, so stop. The last number said is nine.
4. So $6 + 3 = 9$.

blocks.body: Find $12 - 8$ by counting on.
blocks.solution:
1. $12 - 8$ asks: 8 and how many more make 12?
2. Start at eight and count on to twelve: nine (1), ten (2), eleven (3), twelve (4).
3. That is 4 counts.
4. So $12 - 8 = 4$. Check: $8 + 4 = 12$.

items.hint: Say five, then count three more.
Start at nine and count back three.

items.q: Draw a number line from 0 to 10 and show $4 + 5$ with hops of one.
items.hint: Start at 4 and make 5 hops to the right.
items.solution: From 4 the hops land on 5, 6, 7, 8, 9. So $4 + 5 = 9$.

items.hint: Start from the larger number.
items.solution: Start at eight and count two more: nine, ten. $2 + 8 = 10$.

items.hint: 12 and how many more make 15?

items.q: Sam says that to find $14 - 11$ he will count back 11 steps from 14. Suggest a quicker way, and give the answer.
items.hint: Counting on from 11 is only a few steps.
items.solution: Count on from 11 to 14: twelve, thirteen, fourteen, which is 3 counts. So $14 - 11 = 3$; this needs 3 counts instead of 11.

blocks.body:
- To count on, say the first number and count on the second.
- To count back, start at the first number and count back.
- To subtract, you can count on from the smaller number to the larger one; the number of counts is the difference.
- On a number line, adding hops right and subtracting hops left.

blocks.title: Subtraction undoes addition
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to use an addition fact to find a subtraction, find a missing number in an equation, and check a subtraction by adding.

Try this. Put 7 cups on the table and add 2. Now take the 2 away again. How many cups are there?

blocks.title: Addition and subtraction are inverse operations
blocks.body: Taking away what was added brings you back to where you started, and adding back what was taken away does the same: $$7 + 2 = 9 \text{ and } 9 - 2 = 7.$$ So every subtraction is a missing-number addition. Here a question mark stands for a number we do not know yet: $9 - 2$ asks $2 + ? = 9$.

Start with 7 cups and put 2 more down: now there are 9. If you then pick up those same 2 cups, the cups that stay are the 7 you started with. So $9 - 2 = 7$. In the other direction, the difference $9 - 2$ is the number of cups that, together with the 2, make 9, which is the missing number in $2 + ? = 9$. (This is the link between parts and wholes on [[composing-decomposing-numbers]]: one whole and two parts give two additions and two subtractions.)

blocks.title: A missing number
blocks.body: A box or a question mark can stand for a number we do not know yet: $6 + \square = 8$ asks what number goes with 6 to make 8. The missing number can be in any place: $\square + 5 = 9$, $8 - \square = 3$, $7 = \square - 2$.
Find the missing number: $6 + \square = 8$.
blocks.solution:
1. The question asks: 6 and how many more make 8?
2. Count on from 6: seven (1), eight (2).
3. That is 2 counts, so the missing number is 2.
4. Check: $6 + 2 = 8$. The same fact gives $8 - 6 = 2$.

blocks.body: Find $16 - 9$ by using an addition fact.
blocks.solution:
1. $16 - 9$ asks: 9 and how many make 16?
2. Think of an addition fact with 9 that makes 16. 9 and 1 make 10, and 10 and 6 make 16, so 9 and $1 + 6 = 7$ make 16: $9 + 7 = 16$.
3. So $16 - 9 = 7$.
4. Check by adding: $7 + 9 = 16$.

blocks.title: Check a subtraction by adding
blocks.body: Letters can stand for numbers. If $a - b = c$ then $c + b = a$. For example, $9 - 2 = 7$ and $7 + 2 = 9$. So to check a subtraction, add the answer to the number you took away. You should get the number you started with.
$c$ is what is left when $b$ is taken from $a$. Putting the $b$ back with what is left gives all of $a$ again.

blocks.title: Order matters in subtraction
blocks.body: $3 + 5$ and $5 + 3$ are both 8, but $5 - 3$ and $3 - 5$ are not the same. $5 - 3 = 2$: from 5 take away 3. With whole numbers you cannot take 5 away from 3. The England programme of study asks Year 2 pupils to show that addition can be done in any order and subtraction cannot.
Is $43 - 26 = 17$ right? Check by adding.
blocks.solution:
1. Add the answer to the number taken away: $17 + 26$.
2. Tens: $10 + 20 = 30$. Ones: $7 + 6 = 13$.
3. $30 + 13 = 43$.
4. We got back 43, the number we started with, so $43 - 26 = 17$ is right.

items.a: No. $6 - 2 = 4$, but 6 cannot be taken from 2 with whole numbers.

items.q: Write two subtraction facts that come from $3 + 6 = 9$.
items.hint: Take away one part from the whole.
Count on from 4 to 11.
items.solution: Five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, eleven is 7 counts. $4 + 7 = 11$, so the missing number is 7.

items.hint: What do you take from 10 to leave 4? Or: 4 and how many make 10?
Add back the 5 that was taken away.

items.q: Use an addition fact to find $14 - 8$.
items.hint: 8 and how many make 14?

items.q: Jo says $52 - 17 = 45$. Check by adding and say whether she is right.
items.hint: Add 45 and 17.

blocks.body:
- Subtraction undoes addition: $7 + 2 = 9$ and $9 - 2 = 7$.
- A subtraction can be found as a missing addend: $9 - 2$ asks $2 + ? = 9$.
- A missing number can be in any place in an equation.
- Check a subtraction by adding the answer to the number taken away.
- Addition can be done in any order; subtraction cannot.

blocks.title: Adding and subtracting within 20
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to add and subtract numbers up to 20 by making a ten, by using doubles, and by going through ten.

Try this. Fill a ten frame with 9 counters, so 1 square is empty. Now you need to add 5 more counters. Where does the first one go? How many are then left over?

blocks.title: Making a ten
blocks.body: To add to a number close to 10, such as 7, 8 or 9, split the other number so that one part fills up a ten: $$8 + 6 = 8 + 2 + 4$$ $$= 10 + 4 = 14.$$

Put the 8 counters and the 6 counters on two ten frames, filling the first frame first. 8 counters leave 2 empty squares, so 2 of the 6 counters fill the first frame, making 10. The other $6 - 2 = 4$ counters go into the second frame. A full ten and 4 more is 14 ([[place-value]]).

blocks.alt: Two ten frames. The first has 8 black counters and 2 blue striped counters, so it is full, labelled 8 + 2 = 10. The second has 4 blue striped counters in its top row, labelled 4 more.

blocks.title: Doubles and near doubles
blocks.body: A double adds a number to itself, such as $6 + 6 = 12$ or $7 + 7 = 14$. A sum of two numbers that differ by 1 is a near double: $$6 + 7 = 6 + 6 + 1 = 13.$$
7 is 6 and 1 more. So 6 + 7 is 6 + 6 with 1 more on top: $12 + 1 = 13$. In the same way $7 + 8 = 7 + 7 + 1 = 14 + 1 = 15$.

blocks.title: Subtracting through ten
blocks.body: To take away from a teen number, first take away down to 10, then take away the rest: $$13 - 4 = 13 - 3 - 1$$ $$= 10 - 1 = 9.$$ Or count on to 10 and then past it: for $15 - 8$, from 8 to 10 is 2 and from 10 to 15 is 5, so $15 - 8 = 2 + 5 = 7$.

13 is a ten and 3 ones. Taking away 4 means taking away the 3 ones first, which leaves the ten, and then 1 more from the ten, which leaves 9. Taking away 4 in two steps, 3 and then 1, takes away 4 altogether, because $3 + 1 = 4$.

blocks.title: Three numbers: look for a ten
blocks.body: When adding three numbers you may add them in any order, so look for two that make 10: $$4 + 7 + 6 = 4 + 6 + 7$$ $$= 10 + 7 = 17.$$ If no two of them make 10, add two of them and then the third: $3 + 4 + 5 = 7 + 5 = 12$.

All the counters are the same whichever group we count first, so the total does not change when we put the 4 and the 6 together first. 4 and 6 make 10, and 10 and 7 make 17. (Why the order and grouping can change is studied on [[properties-of-operations]].)

blocks.title: Ways to find 9 + 5

items.label: Count on
items.body: Say nine, then count five more: ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen.

items.label: Make a ten
items.body: Take 1 from the 5 to fill up the 9: $9 + 1 = 10$, and 4 are left, so $10 + 4 = 14$.

items.label: Use a ten frame
items.body: 9 counters leave one empty square. One of the 5 fills it; the other 4 start a second frame. One full frame and 4 is 14.

items.label: Use a known fact
items.body: $10 + 5 = 15$, and 9 is one less than 10, so $9 + 5$ is one less than 15, which is 14.

blocks.body: Sources describe several ways to get the same sum; the Common Core progressions call the later ones converting to an easier problem.

blocks.title: For adults: methods grow in stages
blocks.body: The Common Core progressions describe three levels: first children count all the objects (or take away objects and count what is left), then they count on, then they turn a problem into an easier one by making a ten or using a double. Children move between levels and may go back to counting with harder numbers. Illustrative Mathematics Grade 1 builds towards fluency within 10 in its first unit and again at the start of its unit on adding and subtracting within 20, where double ten frames show the structure of teen numbers with the ten clearly visible. The England programme of study asks Year 2 pupils to recall addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently.
Find $7 + 5$ by making a ten.
blocks.solution:
1. 7 needs 3 more to make 10.
2. Split 5 into 3 and 2.
3. $7 + 3 = 10$.
4. Add the 2 that are left: $10 + 2 = 12$.
5. So $7 + 5 = 12$.

blocks.body: Find $14 - 6$ by going through ten.
blocks.solution:
1. 14 is a ten and 4 ones.
2. Split 6 into 4 and 2.
3. Take away 4: $14 - 4 = 10$.
4. Take away the other 2: $10 - 2 = 8$.
5. So $14 - 6 = 8$. Check: $8 + 6 = 14$.

items.q: Find $3 + 8 + 7$ by looking for a ten.

items.hint: 8 needs 2 more to make 10.
Which double is close?
items.solution: $5 + 5 = 10$, and 6 is 1 more than 5, so $5 + 6 = 11$ (or $6 + 6 = 12$, one less is 11).

items.hint: First take away 6 to get to 10.

items.q: Find $13 - 9$ by counting on through ten.
items.hint: From 9 to 10, then from 10 to 13.
Look for two numbers that make 10.

items.q: Draw two ten frames to show $6 + 7$. Say how you make a ten.
items.hint: Fill the first frame first.
items.solution: 6 counters leave 4 empty squares. 4 of the 7 fill the first frame, making 10; the other 3 go into the second frame. $6 + 7 = 10 + 3 = 13$.

items.q: Lena knows $7 + 7 = 14$. How can she use it to find $14 - 8$?
items.hint: 8 is one more than 7.
items.solution: $14 - 7 = 7$, and taking away 1 more gives $7 - 1 = 6$. So $14 - 8 = 6$. Check: $6 + 8 = 14$.

blocks.body:
- Make a ten: split one number to fill up the other to 10, as in $8 + 6 = 8 + 2 + 4 = 14$.
- Use doubles and near doubles: $6 + 7 = 6 + 6 + 1 = 13$.
- Go through ten to subtract: $13 - 4 = 13 - 3 - 1 = 9$.
- With three numbers, add two that make 10 first if you can.
- Aim to know all sums and differences within 20.

blocks.title: Story problems
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to draw a bar model for an adding or subtracting story, write an equation for it, and answer the question, even when the unknown number is not at the end.

Try this. Read: "Some ducks were on a pond. 3 more ducks came. Now there are 8 ducks." What do you not know? Act it out with counters before you calculate.

blocks.title: Where the unknown can be
blocks.body:
In each kind of story any one of the three numbers can be the unknown. The Common Core sorts the stories like this (examples in the style of its table):

- Add to, result unknown: 5 ducks, 3 more come. How many now? $5 + 3 = \square$.
- Add to, change unknown: 5 ducks, some more come, now 8. How many came? $5 + \square = 8$.
- Add to, start unknown: some ducks, 3 more come, now 8. How many were there at first? $\square + 3 = 8$.
- Put together, addend unknown: 8 ducks, 5 are white and the rest are brown. How many are brown? $5 + \square = 8$.
- Compare, difference unknown: Ana has 8 shells, Ben has 5. How many more does Ana have? $5 + \square = 8$ or $8 - 5 = \square$.
- Compare, bigger or smaller unknown: Ben has 5 shells; Ana has 3 more than Ben. How many does Ana have? $5 + 3 = \square$.

Take from stories have the same three unknowns: result, change and start.

- Take from, result unknown: 8 ducks, 3 swim away. How many now? $8 - 3 = \square$.
- Take from, change unknown: 8 ducks, some swim away, 5 are left. How many swam away? $8 - \square = 5$.
- Take from, start unknown: some ducks, 3 swim away, 5 are left. How many were there at first? $\square - 3 = 5$.

blocks.title: Bar model
blocks.body: A bar model (also called a tape diagram) draws each amount as a bar. In a put together story the bars of the parts are laid end to end under the bar of the whole. In a compare story the two bars start at the same place, and the difference is the piece by which the longer bar sticks out. The bars do not need to be measured; they only show which amount is bigger.

blocks.title: Choosing the operation
blocks.body: Once the story is drawn, look at what is unknown. If the unknown is a whole, the long bar made of the parts, add the parts. If the unknown is one part, subtract the known part from the whole (or count on from the known part up to the whole). In a compare story the longer bar is the shorter bar and the difference together: if the longer amount is unknown, add; if the shorter amount or the difference is unknown, subtract.

In a bar model the whole bar is exactly as long as the parts laid end to end. Putting parts together is addition. When one part is missing, it is what is left of the whole after the known part, which is a subtraction, and by the section 'Subtraction undoes addition' also the missing addend. A compare story is the same picture: the longer bar is the shorter bar with the difference added on.

blocks.title: For adults: "more" does not always mean add
blocks.body: Compare stories are among the hardest kinds. In "Lucy has 3 fewer apples than Julie. Lucy has 5. How many does Julie have?" the word fewer suggests subtracting, but the answer is $5 + 3 = 8$. The Common Core progressions list four harder subtypes: add to and take from with the start unknown (such as $\square + 3 = 8$), and compare stories with the bigger amount unknown in "fewer" wording or the smaller amount unknown in "more" wording. Children should work with them in Grade 1 but need not master them until Grade 2.

blocks.title: For adults: the equation should match the story
blocks.body: Illustrative Mathematics notes that many equations can often be written for one story, and that children should focus on explaining how their equation matches the story. For 11 children of whom 7 are girls, both $7 + \square = 11$ and $11 - 7 = \square$ match. Explaining the match matters more than using one particular equation or method.

blocks.title: Word phrases for adding and subtracting

rows.text: plus, sum, increased by, more than, total of, added to. "8 more than 7" is $7 + 8$.
minus, difference, decreased by, less than, subtracted from. "5 less than 8" is $8 - 5$, and "1 subtracted from 6" is $6 - 1$: here the order is reversed from the words.
The titles of its Number, Addition and Subtraction segments speak of aggregation and partitioning, augmentation and reduction, comparison of quantities, and subtraction as difference.

blocks.body: Books list phrases that tell you which operation to use. Be careful with the order of the numbers.
Some children were in the park. 4 children went home. Now there are 9 children in the park. How many children were there at first?
blocks.solution:
1. This is a take from story with the start unknown: $\square - 4 = 9$.
2. Draw a bar for the children at first. It is made of the 9 who stayed and the 4 who went home.
3. So the whole is $9 + 4$.
4. $9 + 4 = 13$ (make a ten: $9 + 1 = 10$, then 3 more).
5. Answer: 13 children were in the park at first. Check: $13 - 4 = 9$.

blocks.body: Mo has 12 marbles. Pia has 7 marbles. How many fewer marbles does Pia have than Mo?
blocks.solution:
1. This is a compare story with the difference unknown.
2. Draw Mo's bar 12 long and Pia's bar 7 long, starting at the same place. The difference is the piece of Mo's bar that Pia's does not reach.
3. $12 - 7$: count on from 7 to 10 (3), then to 12 (2 more). $3 + 2 = 5$.
4. Answer: Pia has 5 fewer marbles. Check: $7 + 5 = 12$.

blocks.body: A bus has 23 people. At the first stop 8 people get off. At the second stop 5 people get on. How many people are on the bus now?
blocks.solution:
1. This is a two-step problem: first a take from, then an add to.
2. Step 1: $23 - 8$. Go through 20: $23 - 3 = 20$, then $20 - 5 = 15$.
3. Step 2: $15 + 5 = 20$.
4. Answer: 20 people are on the bus. The Common Core asks for two-step problems like this in Grade 2.

items.q: Write an equation with a box: 6 birds, some more come, now 10 birds.
Tom has 9 cards and Jen has 4 more than Tom. How many does Jen have?
There are 7 red fish and 6 blue fish in a tank. How many fish are there?
items.hint: Put together, total unknown.
items.solution: $7 + 6$: $7 + 3 = 10$, then 3 more is 13. There are 13 fish.

items.q: Ben has 4 red, 5 blue and 6 green marbles. How many marbles does he have?
items.hint: Three numbers: look for two that make 10.

items.q: Kai had 15 grapes. He ate some. Now he has 9. How many did he eat?
items.hint: Take from, change unknown: $15 - \square = 9$.
items.solution: 9 and how many make 15? $9 + 6 = 15$. Kai ate 6 grapes.

items.q: Translate and work out: "the difference of 14 and 6" and "6 subtracted from 14".
items.hint: One keeps the order of the words, the other reverses it.

items.q: Ella has 5 fewer beads than Ravi. Ella has 8 beads. How many beads does Ravi have?
items.hint: Who has more? Draw the two bars.
items.solution: Ravi has more: his bar is Ella's 8 and 5 more. $8 + 5 = 13$ beads.

items.q: Some books were on a shelf. Mum put 6 more on it. Now there are 14. How many books were there at first?
items.hint: Start unknown: $\square + 6 = 14$.

items.q: Write two different equations for this story and solve it: 11 children, 7 of them are girls. How many are boys?
items.hint: One equation with $+$ and a box, one with $-$.
items.solution: $7 + \square = 11$ and $11 - 7 = \square$. The box is 4: there are 4 boys.

items.q: A shop has 30 apples. It sells 12 in the morning and 9 in the afternoon. How many apples are left?
items.hint: Two steps: two take-aways, or add what was sold first.

blocks.body:
- Every adding or subtracting story has three numbers; any one can be unknown.
- Draw the story as a bar model, then look at what is unknown: a whole means add the parts, a missing part means subtract it from the whole.
- Words like fewer or more than can point the wrong way; check with the bar model.
- Several equations can fit one story, such as $7 + \square = 11$ and $11 - 7 = \square$.
- Two-step problems are solved one step at a time.

blocks.title: Bigger numbers: tens and hundreds
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to add and subtract two-digit and three-digit numbers in your head or with a drawing, by working with tens and ones (and hundreds), including when you need to make or break a ten.

Try this. Build 37 and 25 with towers of ten cubes and single cubes. Put them together. How many towers and how many single cubes do you have? Can you make another tower?

blocks.title: Adding and subtracting tens
blocks.body: Tens add and subtract like ones: 3 tens and 4 tens are 7 tens, so $$30 + 40 = 70, \quad 70 - 40 = 30.$$ In the same way 3 hundreds and 4 hundreds are 7 hundreds: $300 + 400 = 700$. Adding 10 to a number makes its tens digit one larger, and adding 100 makes its hundreds digit one larger: $34 + 10 = 44$ and $345 + 100 = 445$. Taking away 10 makes the tens digit one smaller: $34 - 10 = 24$. (When the digit is 9 a new place is needed: $94 + 10 = 104$.)
30 is 3 towers of ten and 40 is 4 towers of ten. Putting them together gives 7 towers, which is 70. This is the fact $3 + 4 = 7$ with every object being a ten instead of a one ([[place-value]]).

blocks.solution:
1. $38 + 20$: 3 tens and 2 tens are 5 tens, and the 8 ones stay. So $38 + 20 = 58$.
2. $38 + 5$: 38 needs 2 more to make 40. Split 5 into 2 and 3: $38 + 2 = 40$, $40 + 3 = 43$. So $38 + 5 = 43$.
3. $345 - 200$: 3 hundreds take away 2 hundreds leaves 1 hundred, and the 4 tens and 5 ones stay. So $345 - 200 = 145$.

blocks.title: Add like units
blocks.body: To add two-digit numbers, add tens to tens and ones to ones. If the ones make 10 or more, make a new ten from 10 of them: $$37 + 25 = 50 + 12$$ $$= 60 + 2 = 62.$$

Every number is its tens and its ones: 37 is 3 tens and 7 ones, 25 is 2 tens and 5 ones. Putting them together, there are $3 + 2 = 5$ tens and $7 + 5 = 12$ ones. Twelve ones are one ten and 2 ones, so we can bundle 10 of the ones into a new ten: 6 tens and 2 ones, which is 62. Nothing was added or lost; the cubes were only regrouped.

blocks.caption: 37 + 25 with base-ten blocks. 37 is 3 tens and 7 ones (plain); 25 is 2 tens and 5 ones (striped). Together they make 5 tens and 12 ones; 10 of the ones are bundled into a new ten (dashed outline), giving 6 tens and 2 ones, which is 62.
blocks.alt: Left: three plain rods of ten squares and seven plain single squares, labelled 37. A plus sign. Two blue striped rods and five blue striped single squares, labelled 25. An equals sign. Right: six rods, the last one outlined with a red dashed box labelled new ten, and two single squares, labelled 62.

blocks.title: Ways to add 37 + 25

items.label: Tens, then ones
items.body: Add the tens, $30 + 20 = 50$; add the ones, $7 + 5 = 12$; then $50 + 12 = 62$.

items.label: Make a ten first
items.body: Take 3 from the 5 ones of 25 to make 37 up to 40: $37 + 3 = 40$. Add the other 2: 42. Then add the 20: $42 + 20 = 62$.

items.label: Add on by place
items.body: Keep 37 whole and add the tens of 25: $37 + 20 = 57$. Then add the 5 ones, as 3 and 2: $57 + 3 = 60$, $60 + 2 = 62$.

items.label: Number line jumps
items.body: On a number line, jump from 37 by 20 to 57, then by 3 to 60, then by 2 to 62.

blocks.body: Illustrative Mathematics Grade 1 shows children who add like units, make a ten first, and add on by place; an open number line gives a fourth picture of the same sum.

blocks.title: Subtract like units, breaking a ten when needed
blocks.body: To subtract, take tens from tens and ones from ones. If there are not enough ones, break one ten into 10 ones first: $$43 - 26: \ 43 = 30 + 13,$$ $$13 - 6 = 7, \ 30 - 20 = 10,$$ so $43 - 26 = 17$.

43 is 4 tens and 3 ones. We cannot take 6 ones from 3 ones, so we change one of the tens into 10 ones: now there are 3 tens and 13 ones, still 43. From 13 ones take 6, leaving 7. From 3 tens take 2, leaving 1. One ten and 7 ones is 17. Check: $17 + 26 = 43$.

Right: three rods, two of them struck through in red, and thirteen single squares in columns of five, three plain and ten blue striped; the last six squares are crossed out in red. Labels: 3 tens, 13 ones; take away 2 tens, 6 ones; left: 1 ten, 7 ones = 17.

blocks.title: Two ways to subtract 43 - 26
blocks.body: The same difference can be found by breaking a ten or by counting on from the smaller number.

items.label: Break a ten
items.body: Change 1 ten of 43 into 10 ones: 3 tens and 13 ones. Take 2 tens and 6 ones. 1 ten and 7 ones are left, which is 17.

items.label: Count on
items.body: Start at 26 and count on to 43 in jumps: 4 to reach 30, 10 to reach 40, 3 to reach 43. The jumps are $4 + 10 + 3 = 17$, so the difference is 17.

blocks.title: Compensation
blocks.body: Moving some from one number to the other does not change a sum: $$28 + 16 = 30 + 14 = 44.$$ For a difference, add the same amount to both numbers (or take the same amount from both): $74 - 38 = 76 - 40 = 36$.

In $28 + 16$, move 2 from the 16 to the 28. The total number of things is the same; only the parts change, to 30 and 14. For $74 - 38$ think of the difference between two towers, 74 and 38 cubes tall. Adding 2 cubes to each tower makes them 76 and 40 cubes tall, but one is still sticking out above the other by the same amount, so the difference does not change. NRICH says a number line can give visual support when the compensation method is first introduced.

blocks.title: Three-digit numbers
blocks.body: The same ideas work with hundreds. Add or subtract hundreds to hundreds, tens to tens and ones to ones, and make or break a ten or a hundred when needed: $$245 + 300 = 545,$$ $$456 + 376 = 700 + 120 + 12$$ $$= 832.$$

456 is 4 hundreds, 5 tens and 6 ones; 376 is 3 hundreds, 7 tens and 6 ones. Together: 7 hundreds, 12 tens and 12 ones. 12 ones are 1 ten and 2 ones, and 12 tens are 1 hundred and 2 tens. That gives 8 hundreds, 3 tens and 2 ones, so 832. Ten tens make a hundred just as ten ones make a ten ([[place-value]]).

blocks.title: Written column methods
blocks.body: Writing the numbers one above the other, with ones under ones and tens under tens, gives the column methods (formal written methods in England, the standard algorithm in the United States). They use exactly the regrouping of this section and are taught on [[column-addition-subtraction]].

blocks.title: Names for making and breaking a ten

rows.text: Adding: it says carrying is the same as regrouping by exchanging ten ones for a ten. Subtracting: it says to borrow from the tens place, and also describes this as exchanging a ten for ten ones.
Compose a ten (or a hundred) when adding; decompose a ten (or a hundred) when subtracting.
Its column addition page says regroup when a column reaches ten; its Year 3 column subtraction page says exchange (from tens to ones).

Illustrative Mathematics Grade 1 writes equations across the page on purpose, so children keep thinking about the numbers; OpenStax writes the numbers in columns with the carried digit above the next column.

blocks.body: The step where 10 ones become a ten, or a ten becomes 10 ones, has many names.

blocks.title: Estimate first, then check
blocks.body: The England programme of study asks Year 3 pupils to estimate the answer to a calculation and to use inverse operations to check answers. For $456 + 376$: 456 is close to 460 and 376 is close to 380, so the sum should be close to $460 + 380 = 840$. Afterwards, check with the inverse: $832 - 376 = 456$, the number we started with.
Find $52 + 46$ by working with tens and ones.
blocks.solution:
1. Split both numbers: 52 is $50 + 2$, 46 is $40 + 6$.
2. Tens: $50 + 40 = 90$.
3. Ones: $2 + 6 = 8$. That is less than 10, so no new ten.
4. $90 + 8 = 98$.
5. So $52 + 46 = 98$.

blocks.body: Find $23 + 14 + 36 + 21$ by working with tens and ones.

blocks.solution:
1. 910 is 9 hundreds, 1 ten and 0 ones; 586 is 5 hundreds, 8 tens and 6 ones.
2. Ones: we cannot take 6 from 0, so break the ten: 9 hundreds, 0 tens, 10 ones. $10 - 6 = 4$.
3. Tens: we cannot take 8 from 0, so break a hundred: 8 hundreds, 10 tens. $10 - 8 = 2$.
4. Hundreds: $8 - 5 = 3$.
5. The answer is 3 hundreds, 2 tens and 4 ones: $910 - 586 = 324$.
6. Check: $324 + 586 = 910$.

items.q: $45 + 38$: how many tens and how many ones before you make a new ten?

items.q: A school has 207 pupils. 64 of them go on a trip. How many stay at school? Check your answer.
items.hint: 207 has 0 tens; break a hundred into tens.
items.solution: 207 is 1 hundred, 10 tens and 7 ones. Take 6 tens and 4 ones: 1 hundred, 4 tens, 3 ones, so $207 - 64 = 143$. Check: $143 + 64 = 207$.

blocks.body:
- Tens and hundreds add and subtract like ones: $30 + 40 = 70$.
- Add tens to tens and ones to ones; 10 ones make a new ten.
- To subtract when there are too few ones, break a ten into 10 ones.
- Several methods work for the same sum; a number line can show the jumps.
- Compensation: $28 + 16 = 30 + 14$.
- Estimate first and check with the inverse.
- Several two-digit numbers, even four of them, are added by tens and ones.

blocks.title: Looking ahead
blocks.body:
Everything on this page grows into later mathematics. Written column methods ([[column-addition-subtraction]]) are the make-a-ten and break-a-ten steps done digit by digit, and they work for numbers of any size. Reading $=$ as "is the same as" and finding missing numbers lead to equations and algebra ([[equality-equal-sign]]).

The facts that the order of adding does not matter, that adding 0 changes nothing, and that subtraction undoes addition are the properties of operations ([[properties-of-operations]]). In higher mathematics these same rules, written with letters as $a + b = b + a$ and $a + 0 = a$, are the axioms of a group under addition, and they are taken as the starting point of [[groups]] and of [[rings]]. Allowing subtraction always, even $3 - 5$, needs negative numbers. Adding the same number again and again is the start of [[multiplication]].
